The town’s lost-and-found was in the basement of the library, beside a radiator that worked only in August.

People brought the usual things: umbrellas, gloves, a single roller skate. They also brought things for which there were no forms.

A woman once left a jar on the counter. “My husband’s laugh,” she explained. “It disappeared sometime in March.”

The librarian, whose name was Ada, held the jar to her ear. There was a faint sound inside, like a spoon tapping the rim of a glass.

“We’ll do what we can,” Ada said.

She wrote *LAUGH, HUSBAND’S* on a label and put the jar on a shelf. The woman returned every Tuesday to ask about it. The laugh never grew any louder, but eventually she began staying after Ada went upstairs, sorting the unclaimed gloves into pairs.

There was a boy who had lost the feeling that summer would last forever. Ada found him a chair and a cup of tea. She could not find the feeling, but she did find a photograph someone had left between the pages of an atlas: three children standing in a sprinkler, all of them blurry except for their feet. The boy took it home.

Over the years, the basement filled with such things. A tin containing the smell of a kitchen that had been demolished. A paper bag with a horse’s patience in it. An envelope marked *THE RIGHT WORD FOR WHAT HAPPENED*, which Ada kept near the desk in case anyone came looking.

One morning, the mayor arrived carrying nothing at all.

“I think I’ve lost the town,” he said.

Ada looked past him, up the stairs. Through the library windows she could see the pharmacy, the bus stop, and a man walking a dog in a yellow coat.

“It seems to be where we left it.”

“That’s not what I mean.”

The mayor sat down. The radiator clicked, though it was November.

“There are people here I’ve never met. Shops I don’t go into. Streets I only drive through.” He rubbed his forehead. “Yesterday someone asked me where the old swimming pool used to be, and I had no idea. I’ve lived here my whole life.”

Ada considered this. Then she took a blank label from the drawer and handed it to him.

“What should I write?” he asked.

“I don’t know yet. Put your coat on. We’ll go and ask.”

They started at the bus stop, where the man with the dog was now waiting. He knew where the swimming pool had been, and that the woman at the bakery had taught lessons there. At the bakery, the woman told them about the time a swan landed in the deep end and refused to leave. She sent them to the butcher, who had photographs.

By lunchtime, the mayor had filled both sides of the label and borrowed a larger sheet of paper. Ada went back to the library. The mayor stayed for a sandwich at the butcher’s counter and returned the next day to collect the photographs.

After that, people began coming into the library with stories about the town. Ada found a box for them, then another. Some accounts contradicted each other; a few had dates or names crossed out and corrected. The mayor came by on Fridays to read the new ones.

One afternoon, Ada found a jar on the counter. It was empty except for a note:

*He laughed at breakfast today. I thought you might need the jar.*

She washed it and put it beneath the desk. It was a good jar, with a lid that still screwed on straight. Someone would be sure to need it.
